newsitem.title: USA: Clinton partially backs Senate encryption bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton partially backs Senate encryption bill.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said in a letter to Senate majority leader Trent Lott that he partially supports a Senate bill to slightly relax U.S. export limits on computer encoding technology.
But the President, in the July 24 letter obtained by Reuters on Wednesday, said the elements he backed dealt with domestic public computer networks, rather than export controls.

The bill, drafted by Nebraska Democrat Bob Kerrey, "contains many elements I support," Clinton wrote. "In particular, I welcome the bill's explicit recognition of the need to balance competing objectives and of the potential for key recovery to become a market-driven mechanism to achieve that balance."

The administration has long been seen as opposed to any legislation to relax export controls on encryption, computer programs that scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key."

Instead, the administration favors development of encryption products that allow the government to decode any message by gaining access to the software keys, a process known as key recovery. Law enforcement agencies want key recovery to allow them to crack the communications of criminals.

The Kerrey bill would require that any computer products bought by the government or funded by government research grants include key recovery features. The bill also shields from liability certain companies that deal with encryption keys if the companies use key recovery.
Software companies and civil liberties advocates among others have rejected the Kerrey bill as unworkable and a threat to the privacy and security of people using the Internet.
But Clinton said Kerrey's bill could form the basis of needed legislation.

"We need legislation this year to assure the trust and confidence necessary for electronic commerce in the United States to reach its full potential," the President wrote. "I look forward to working with Congress on (the bill) to arrive at a satisfactory consensus on this important challenge."

Kerrey's bill was approved by the Senate Commerce Committee in June but in an unusual legislative maneuver has not yet been formally "filed" by the committee. Staffer said they are discussing changing the already approved legislation before it is filed. The Senate Judiciary Committee has asked for jurisdiction over the Kerrey bill and may draft its own legislation.

Clinton continues to strongly oppose a bill in the House written by Virginia Republican Bob Goodlatte that would virtually eliminate encryption export controls and prohibit the government from imposing mandatory key recovery within the United States, administration officials said.

A number of reports by cryptography experts have questioned key recovery technology and warned that it may introduce new vulnerabilities into computer networks. Some companies are offering key recovery products or plan to soon, although not all meet the needs of law enforcement officials.
